analysis.one_liner: Tightens the rule limiting how much federal student aid for-profit colleges can collect.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised the required non-federal revenue share for for-profit colleges from 10% to 15% and ended a two-year grace period before losing aid eligibility, was referred to committee on June 10, 2019 and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently lets for-profit colleges get up to 90% of their revenue from federal student aid, and a school only loses access to that aid after breaking the rule two years in a row. This bill would have required at least 15% of revenue to come from sources other than federal funds, tightened the accounting rules so schools couldn't pad the number with their own loans and scholarships, counted GI Bill housing stipends as non-federal revenue, and cut off federal aid eligibility immediately for schools that don't comply. It died in the House Education and Labor Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Students enrolled at for-profit colleges, who would face schools with less dependence on federal loan dollars and schools that fail the test losing access to federal aid immediately instead of after two consecutive years, and taxpayers, who fund the federal aid that for-profit colleges would have to rely on less heavily.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum share of revenue for-profit colleges must get from non-federal sources from 10% to 15%, reducing the share of school income that comes directly from federal student aid.

Tightens what counts as non-federal revenue: institutional loans no longer count, institutional scholarships only count if funded from an outside source with no affiliation to the school, and only a narrow set of student-benefiting activities count as revenue.

Makes failing the 85/15 rule an immediate loss of eligibility for federal student aid programs, replacing current law where a school must violate the rule for two consecutive years before losing eligibility.

Requires the Education Secretary to report to Congress annually, starting by July 1, 2020, on the amount and percentage of federal and non-federal revenue for each for-profit college receiving federal aid.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies and their investors, whose federal student aid revenue would be capped lower and who could lose access to federal aid immediately after a single year of non-compliance; some enrolled students could be affected if a school closed abruptly.

drawbacks.text: The bill still permits GI Bill monthly housing stipends to be counted as non-federal revenue, so schools serving veterans can continue relying on those federal dollars to meet the 15% threshold.

Immediate loss of federal aid eligibility gives a non-complying school no transition period; without a teach-out provision in the bill, students enrolled at a school that loses eligibility could be left without a pathway to finish their programs.
Even at 85/15, for-profit colleges could still draw 85% of revenue from federal student aid, so the underlying dependence on federal dollars remains largely intact.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have meaningfully reduced taxpayer exposure to for-profit colleges that rely almost entirely on federal aid and would have sped up consequences for schools that break the rule. Its main weakness is the carve-out letting GI Bill housing stipends count as non-federal revenue, which preserves a federal funding stream for schools that target veteran students, and the lack of a transition mechanism for enrolled students at schools that would lose eligibility.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the POST Act on June 10, 2019, with Reps. Jackson Lee and Cisneros as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day; that referral was the last action recorded.
The bill attracted 5 cosponsors in total, all Democrats, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The for-profit college industry is better off, having kept the existing 90/10 rule with its two-year grace period and its existing accounting loopholes intact for another two-year Congress; federal student aid dollars continued flowing under the old rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit college companies and their investors

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled after the June 10, 2019 referral.

against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the two-year Congress.

against.what_they_did: Opposed tightening of the 90/10 rule and its loopholes, which would cap its federal revenue share and speed up loss of aid eligibility.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so no partisan split is on record; the bill was sponsored only by House Democrats (5 of 231) and died in committee without any recorded opposition or support.

industries.note: The bill would cap their federal student aid revenue at 85% instead of 90% and close accounting loopholes such as counting institutional loans and scholarships as revenue, with immediate loss of aid eligibility for a single year of non-compliance instead of after two years. It matters for ordinary people because these schools' revenue comes overwhelmingly from federal loans taken on by students, many of whom end up with debt from programs that don't pay off.

The bill counts most federal funds against the 15% threshold but carves out Post-9/11 GI Bill monthly housing stipends, so schools serving veterans can keep counting that federal money as non-federal revenue. This preserves a revenue stream for for-profit schools that enroll veteran students rather than reducing their federal dependence.
